chapters.category: Ethiopic textual tradition • Modern English research translation
chapters.title: Chapter 103 — Joy Is Prepared for the Righteous
chapters.sourceNote: Translated afresh into clear modern English from the earliest primary-language witnesses responsibly available for this chapter. No surviving Aramaic manuscript preserves wording from Chapter 103. The fourth-century Chester Beatty–Michigan Papyrus XII governs all wording it preserves throughout the chapter. The complete Ethiopic (Geʽez) text in August Dillmann’s 1851 critical edition, Liber Henoch Aethiopice, printed pages 88–89, fills physical or textually damaged places in the Greek papyrus and confirms the complete fifteen-verse sequence. No modern English translation was used as the translation base, no commentary was used as Scripture, and no text absent from these primary witnesses was supplied.

verses.text: Now I swear to you, the righteous, by the glory of the Great One, by his honored kingdom, and by his greatness; I swear to you—
verses.study: Enoch binds the coming assurance to the majesty and rule of the Great One. The solemn oath answers the despair voiced at the close of the previous chapter.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 32:40 — a solemn divine oath guarantees what follows
Hebrews 6:13–18 — an oath provides strong encouragement for those who hope

verses.text: I know this mystery. I have read the heavenly tablets, I have seen the holy books, and I found written and engraved in them concerning you—
verses.study: The promised reversal is not wishful consolation. Enoch presents it as a disclosed heavenly mystery fixed in the holy record.
crossReferences: Daniel 7:10 — heavenly books are opened before the court
Malachi 3:16 — a book of remembrance is written before the Lord

verses.text: that every good thing, joy, and honor have been prepared and written down for the spirits of those who died in righteousness. Abundant good will be given to you in recompense for your labor, and your portion will be better than the portion of the living.
verses.study: Earthly hardship has neither erased the righteous nor emptied their work of value. Their prepared portion exceeds the visible advantages of those still living.
crossReferences: Isaiah 64:4 — God acts for those who wait for him
Hebrews 11:13–16 — the faithful seek a better, heavenly country

verses.text: The spirits of you who have died in righteousness will live and rejoice; their spirits will not perish, and their remembrance will remain before the Great One through all generations of eternity. Therefore, do not fear their abuse.
verses.study: The sinners called the righteous forgotten and extinguished, but the heavenly record declares life, joy, and permanent remembrance before God.
crossReferences: Psalm 112:6 — the righteous are remembered forever
Luke 20:37–38 — all live to God, who is God of the living

verses.text: Woe to you sinners when you die in your sins! Those like you will say about you, ‘Blessed were the sinners; they saw all their days.
verses.study: The judgment oracle exposes how the wicked praise one another by measuring blessing only through the ease and pleasure visible during mortal life.
crossReferences: Psalm 10:3 — the wicked praise greedy desire
Luke 16:25 — remembered earthly good does not determine the final state

verses.text: Now they have died in prosperity and wealth. They saw no distress or slaughter during their lifetime; they died in honor, and no judgment was carried out upon them while they lived.’
verses.study: Prosperity, safety, and public honor can conceal accountability for a time. The absence of immediate judgment is not acquittal.
crossReferences: Psalm 73:3–5 — the arrogant appear prosperous and free from ordinary trouble
Ecclesiastes 8:11–13 — delayed judgment emboldens sinners but does not secure them

verses.text: Know that their souls will be made to descend into Sheol; there they will be wretched, and their distress will be great.
verses.study: The hidden destination overturns the public verdict pronounced at their graves. Honor among people gives way to great distress in Sheol.
crossReferences: Psalm 49:16–19 — earthly glory cannot prevent descent to the dead
Luke 16:22–24 — earthly luxury is followed by anguish in the realm of the dead

verses.text: Their spirits will enter darkness, snares, and a burning flame, where there is great judgment throughout all generations of eternity. Woe to you, for you will have no peace.
verses.study: Darkness, confinement, fire, and enduring judgment name the sinners’ true inheritance. The repeated absence of peace answers their temporary security.
crossReferences: Isaiah 50:11 — those who kindle destructive fire lie down in torment
Jude 6–7 — darkness and fire portray reserved judgment

verses.text: You righteous and good who are alive, do not say, ‘In the days of our distress we endured hard labor and saw every kind of trouble. We have been consumed and diminished, and our spirit has grown small.
verses.study: The address now records the faithful community’s own lament. Exhaustion can shrink the spirit until suffering seems to be the whole truth.
crossReferences: Psalm 44:23–26 — the oppressed faithful ask God to rise and help
2 Corinthians 4:8–9 — affliction presses the faithful without finally destroying them

verses.text: We have been destroyed, and there was no one to help us even with a word. We were powerless and found nothing. We were crushed and ruined, and we no longer hoped to see life from one day to the next.
verses.study: The lament does not minimize abandonment, helplessness, or the loss of ordinary hope. Its honesty makes the heavenly promise a direct answer to real oppression.
crossReferences: Psalm 142:4–6 — no refuge or helper appears to the afflicted
2 Corinthians 1:8–10 — despairing even of life becomes the setting for deliverance

verses.text: We hoped to become the head, but we became the tail. We labored and had no mastery over what our work produced. We became food for sinners and the lawless, and they made their yoke heavy upon us.
verses.study: Oppression reverses rightful order and confiscates the fruit of labor. The images of prey and a heavy yoke show exploitation as both economic and violent.
crossReferences: Deuteronomy 28:13, 44 — head and tail describe a reversal of communal standing
Isaiah 3:14–15 — leaders are condemned for crushing the poor

verses.text: Those who hated and struck us ruled over us. We bowed our neck to those who hated us, but they showed us no compassion.
verses.study: The righteous describe domination without mercy: enemies hold power, force submission, and refuse the compassion that might restrain cruelty.
crossReferences: Lamentations 5:5, 8 — exhausted people are ruled without rescue
James 2:13 — judgment is without mercy to the one who has shown no mercy

verses.text: We wanted to get away from them so that we might escape and find rest, but we found no place to flee and be safe from them.
verses.study: Every earthly route to rest appears closed. The lack of safe refuge underscores why vindication must come from the heavenly Judge.
crossReferences: Psalm 55:6–8 — the afflicted longs to fly away and find rest
Lamentations 1:3 — amid persecution there is no resting place

verses.text: In our distress we complained to the rulers and cried out against those who devoured us, but they paid no attention to our cries and would not listen to our voice.
verses.study: Institutions meant to hear the harmed instead ignore them. The repeated cry turns human judicial failure into evidence for divine review.
crossReferences: Exodus 5:15–18 — oppressed workers appeal to authority and receive no relief
James 5:4 — the withheld wages of laborers cry out before the Lord

verses.text: They helped those who robbed and devoured us and those who reduced our number. They concealed the violence against us; they did not remove the yoke of those who consumed, scattered, and murdered us. They hid their killing, and they did not remember that sinners had raised their hands against us.
verses.study: The lament ends with official complicity: authorities assist plunderers, hide bloodshed, and erase the record of violence. Yet the chapter’s opening has already declared that heaven’s record does not forget.
crossReferences: Isaiah 10:1–4 — unjust rulers deprive the vulnerable and become partners in plunder
Habakkuk 1:2–4 — violence persists because corrupted justice does not go forth

explanation.heading: Chapter teaching and context
paragraphs: Chapter 103 answers the apparent equality of righteous and wicked deaths described in Chapter 102. Enoch swears by the Great One’s glory and kingdom that a hidden heavenly record exists. What earthly observers call extinction is not the whole account.

The tablets declare that good, joy, honor, and recompense are prepared for those who die in righteousness. Their spirits live, their remembrance remains before the Great One, and their future portion is better than the portion now visible among the living. Divine remembrance reverses the sinners’ claim that the righteous have vanished.

The chapter then exposes the opposite error made at a sinner’s death. Friends may call the prosperous sinner blessed because distress and judgment were absent during life. Yet delayed judgment is not canceled judgment: the unseen destination is described as Sheol, darkness, confinement, fire, and the loss of peace.

Verses 9–15 preserve the righteous community’s lament in full. They have been exhausted, deprived of their labor, subjected to a heavy yoke, denied refuge, ignored by rulers, and attacked by people protected by those rulers. The chapter does not rebuke them for naming injustice; it places their testimony beside the heavenly books, where concealed violence and forgotten victims remain known before the Great One.

crossReferences: 1 Enoch 102:4–11 — righteous death appears futile before the heavenly disclosure
1 Enoch 104:1–6 — the righteous are again assured of heavenly light and remembrance
Psalm 9:12–18 — God remembers bloodshed and does not forget the afflicted
Psalm 73:17–24 — the sanctuary reveals destinies hidden by present appearances
Daniel 7:9–10 — the heavenly court sits and the books are opened
Malachi 3:16–18 — a heavenly record preserves the distinction between righteous and wicked
Luke 16:19–26 — death unveils a reversal concealed during earthly life
2 Corinthians 4:16–18 — present affliction is weighed against unseen eternal glory
James 5:1–6 — oppressive wealth and withheld wages await judgment
Revelation 6:9–11 — murdered witnesses remain known and call for just judgment
